title: Britain Once Taxed Sunlight
description: An original 60-second narrated 3D history short about the British window tax, responses recorded in historical tax rolls, and the distinction between tax avoidance and symmetrical facade design.
narration_text: What if the windows in your house came with a tax bill? In 1696, England introduced a tax linked to the number of windows in a home. More windows could mean a larger bill. Assessors counted the openings, and the number went into the household's assessment. Some owners responded by closing windows to reduce what they owed. Surviving tax records even note openings that had been closed. But a bricked-up window doesn't always prove tax avoidance. Some Georgian houses used blank windows to keep their facades symmetrical. So historians have to distinguish design choices from tax responses. The tax remained for more than 150 years, until it was repealed in 1851. Critics had raised concerns about the effects of dim, poorly ventilated homes. A rule meant to count windows changed how people thought about their walls. Sometimes the biggest effect of a rule is the behaviour it creates.

story.hook: What if the windows in your house came with a tax bill?
beats: Open on a sweeping vertical view of a Georgian street and the visual idea of a window being counted.
Establish 1696 England and show the assessor recording the number of windows.
Move to the householder and reveal the tax assessment as a household cost.
Explain that more windows could mean a larger bill under the banded assessment.
Show one opening being filled with brick as a documented response by some owners.
Cut to historical tax records noting windows that had been closed.
Introduce the counterpoint: a blank window can also be a deliberate architectural choice.
Compare symmetrical Georgian facades so the viewer can see the difference.
Show the repeal in 1851 and the public-health criticism around light and ventilation.
End on a wide restored facade and the idea that rules can change the behaviour they target.
